subject: Business Models
title: Mesopotamian Merchants
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Mesopotamian Merchants.

hook.text: Around 3000 BCE, Mesopotamia developed the world's first merchant class. Trade became a profession.

buildup.text: Merchants carried textiles, metals, and grain along river routes between cities like Ur and Babylon.

discovery.text: They invented clay tablets to record debts and transactions—the birth of written accounting.

twist.text: Writing itself may have been invented for commerce, not poetry. Ledgers came before literature.

climax.text: These merchants created the template for business: track inventory, manage credit, move goods.

punchline.text: The first businesspeople wrote the rules 5,000 years ago.

quiz.question: What did Mesopotamian merchants invent to track transactions?

details.summary: Mesopotamian merchants in ancient Sumer around 3000 BCE created the first formal commercial systems including written contracts, standardized weights, trade credit, interest-bearing loans, and commodity money. These innovations in the Fertile Crescent laid the foundation for all subsequent commerce.
details.whyItMatters: Every commercial concept we use today, from contracts to credit to accounting, traces back to Mesopotamian innovations..
takeaways: Sumerians created written contracts, standardized weights, and trade credit by 3000 BCE
Clay tablets recorded debts, inventory, and commercial agreements in cuneiform
Interest-bearing loans and commodity money systems emerged in ancient Mesopotamia

faq.question: What commercial innovations came from ancient Mesopotamia?
faq.answer: Written commercial contracts on clay tablets, standardized weights and measures for fair exchange, silver-based commodity money, interest-bearing loans for trade ventures, warehouse receipts as proto-currency, and the concept of limited liability for trading partnerships.

faq.question: How did ancient Mesopotamian credit systems work?
faq.answer: Temple and palace institutions provided grain loans to farmers at planting time, repaid with interest after harvest. Merchant traders received silver advances for trade expeditions. Clay tablet contracts specified terms, interest rates, and penalties. Interest rates of 20 to 33 percent were common.
